newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Forty-six killed in fighting in southeast Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Forty-six killed in fighting in southeast Colombia.

text.p: Twenty-one soldiers and up to 25 leftist guerrillas were killed on Friday in fighting in southern Colombia that capped a week-long rebel offensive.

Military spokesmen said the clashes took place in a rural area of southeastern Guaviare province where 21 soldiers and an estimated 25 Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas were killed.

Heavy fighting continued in a remote area of the jungle- covered province known as La Carpa on Friday night and the military spokesmen told Reuters the Air Force was strafing guerrilla positions and targeting some areas for bombing.
The combat zone is about 215 miles (350 km) southeast of Bogota and three hours by riverboat from the provincial capital of San Jose del Guaviare.
There were unconfirmed reports that at least 15 soldiers had been wounded, but officials said further information about casualties was not immediately available.

In central Cundinamarca province, meanwhile, police and military spokesmen said four policemen were killed late on Friday in fighting with suspected FARC rebels who were manning a roadblock about 30 miles (50 km) north of Bogota.
The clash occurred near the town of Zipaquira, famous for an underground cathedral carved out of an abandoned salt mine that is a major a tourist attraction.
Guerrillas launched a nationwide offensive last Friday in which dozens of police and government troops were killed in some of the worst fighting the country has seen this decade.
Twenty-seven soldiers were killed when FARC rebels overran a military base in southwestern Putumayo province and at least 60 are being held as "prisoners of war" after the attack.

The FARC, Colombia's largest rebel group, grew out of peasant militias founded in 1948. It was officially founded as a Marxist, pro-Soviet group in 1964 and has been fighting for more than three decades to topple the Colombian government.
